conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, because the postpartum weeks can bring surprises for every new mom. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team; there’s no judgment, only support. We’ll go through ten gentle questions about the past seven days, and I’ll re-phrase each one so it feels like a normal conversation. When you’re ready, we can begin.

First question: Over the last week, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you smile, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

Hi, Sarah… yeah, I’ve noticed it’s slipped. Things like scrolling through funny videos or grabbing a fancy coffee used to feel nice, but this week they just seem kind of… flat. I’ll still do them while the baby naps, yet I don’t get that little lift I used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most days I can still laugh—like when my partner makes a goofy face to get the baby to smile—but it feels kind of forced on my end, and the laughter fades pretty fast.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Lately, no… I’m not really looking forward to much. Even little plans—like going for a short walk with the stroller—feel more like chores than something nice to anticipate.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a lot. If the baby’s fussy and I can’t settle her right away, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong or I’m not a good enough mom. Same when I burn the toast or forget to switch the laundry—my brain jumps to “This is my fault, I should be better at this.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty often, yeah. Like, I’ll be feeding her and suddenly worry her breathing sounds different, or I’ll lie down and my heart starts racing about whether the crib mattress is too soft—even though I checked it a million times. Nothing’s actually wrong, but I can’t shake the “what-ifs.”
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah. The other night I was just rocking the baby in the nursery and suddenly felt this wave of panic—like something awful was about to happen, even though everything was quiet. My chest got tight and I had to keep telling myself to breathe. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days it feels like I’m barely treading water. I’ll finally get her down for a nap and the minute I start the dishes she’s crying again, or I realize I forgot to eat lunch. I keep thinking, “How am I supposed to keep this up?”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head just keeps spinning with everything I might’ve messed up that day or all the things that could go wrong tomorrow. Even when the baby’s asleep, I’ll stare at the ceiling for an hour or two, and if I do drift off, I wake up at every tiny sound.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. I’ll be folding her tiny clothes or just watching her sleep and this heavy sadness rolls in—like I’m missing something or I’m failing her even when nothing’s actually gone wrong.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
A few times, yeah. Yesterday I burst into tears when she wouldn’t latch—just sat there sobbing with her in my arms. It’s usually when I’m already tired and something small tips me over.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, Sarah—nothing like that. I might feel overwhelmed and useless, but I haven’t thought about hurting myself.

I hear how heavy these early weeks have felt for you-how even simple joys like a funny video or a walk with the stroller now seem distant, how the worries race at night, and how easily the tears come when the baby won't latch. You're working so hard to keep everything afloat while feeling you're "barely treading water," yet you still showed up today to share what's happening inside. That courage matters, and you don't have to carry this alone.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 22, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports absence of anticipatory enjoyment and describes even simple plans as burdensome, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, automatic self-blame for minor mishaps, matching "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive worries that occur "pretty often" and persist despite reassurance, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes spontaneous panic symptoms (sudden dread, chest tightness, need to self-soothe) matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days" and unable to manage basic tasks, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly insomnia with racing thoughts and frequent awakenings, indicating the highest level of sleep difficulty.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports experiencing sadness "pretty much every day this week," indicating persistence and frequency that aligns with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS item scoring: enjoyment 3, laughter 1, self-blame 3, anxiety 3, panic 2, coping 3, sleep 3, sadness 3, crying 1, self-harm 0; total 22. A score ≥14 plus daily mood symptoms for most of the past week meets screening threshold for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> (DSM-5: depressed mood, markedly diminished interest, guilt, sleep disturbance, fatigue, impaired concentration nearly every day). No self-harm ideation on Item 10. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> within the next few days
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>interpersonal therapy</med>, <med>CBT</med>, or <med>sertraline</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Share today's EPDS result with your provider so they can complete a full diagnostic evaluation
4. Arrange practical support-partner, family, or postpartum doula for night feedings and household tasks to protect sleep
5. Practice 5-minute grounding or breathing breaks when panic sensations start; keep baby nearby in a safe spot while you regulate
6. Use the 24-hr <med>Postpartum Support International</med> warm-line (1-800-944-4PPD) for encouragement and local resources
7. Return for EPDS re-screen in 2 weeks to monitor progress after starting treatment
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 22: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: “Sarah” (self-reported)  
Date: [today]  
Source: written questionnaire  

Presenting symptoms endorsed (10-item EPDS-style items):

• Persistent low mood, crying spells, daily sadness (“pretty much every day this week”)  
• Marked anhedonia—no enjoyment/anticipation of activities; laughter feels “forced”  
• Excessive self-blame/guilt (“I’m not a good enough mom”); cognitive distortion pattern  
• Heightened generalized anxiety, somatic tension, heart racing, “what-ifs”  
• Discrete panic episode (tight chest, dread) without identifiable trigger  
• Sleep disturbance linked to ruminations; difficulty initiating/maintaining sleep despite exhaustion  
• Subjective sense of being overwhelmed, “barely treading water,” low coping confidence  

Safety items: Denies thoughts of self-harm (“No… nothing like that”).

Pattern: Symptoms cross the threshold for clinically significant distress; constellation most consistent with probable major depressive episode with anxious features in the postpartum period (differential: postpartum anxiety disorder). No current self-harm ideation; no psychotic content reported.

Risk screening conclusion: High clinical concern for postpartum depression/anxiety; warrants immediate formal assessment (clinical interview, EPDS scoring, differential diagnosis) and discussion of support/intervention options.
